Sample Spaces, Events, and Probability Axioms

Probability and Statistics · Chapter 1 · Revised English review draft · 48 individually worked questions

1. Scope, prerequisites, and source selection

Probability starts by specifying what can happen and which outcomes belong to the question being asked. A numerical answer is meaningful only after that model is fixed. This chapter builds the model from elementary outcomes through event algebra, admissible event families, probability axioms, exact identities, feasibility bounds, and countable-event limits. It includes finite weighted models, ordinary uniform interval and area models, and an interactive two-event model. Combinatorial counting techniques and independence are the next chapter's main subjects; conditional probability, Bayes' rule, random-variable distributions, and expectation have later boundaries. A few small finite enumerations appear here to make modeling precise.

Prerequisites are sets, complements, unions, intersections, disjoint partitions, geometric series, and elementary limits. Whenever an infinite sum or a limit is used, its role is explained. Full measure construction and integration theory are outside this chapter; introducing an event family does not require learning those entire subjects first.

The reviewed core texts are MIT 6.041/6.431 Lecture 1 by John Tsitsiklis; Stanford CS109 Lecture Notes 3 by Lisa Yan, based on Chris Piech's handout; Berkeley Stat 210A's Measure Theory Basics by Will Fithian; and ETH Zurich's Probability Theory by Vincent Tassion, Section 1.1. Oxford's Probability and Computing notes by Elias Koutsoupias provide a fifth written perspective on the union bound. They were selected for complementary chapter coverage after a bounded survey, not simply because four links were available. The source audit records the exact portions read, candidate exclusions, and limitations. All explanations, diagrams, and problem statements below are independently written; source-inspired reasoning types are attributed in the problem-bank introduction.

2. Constructing a sample space before assigning numbers

2.1 Experiment, outcome, and event

An experiment is the process being modeled: for example, rolling a marked die once, observing two ordered coin tosses, or measuring a service duration. A sample space Ω is a nonempty set whose elements describe the mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive elementary outcomes of that process. One execution produces one element ω∈Ω. An event is an admissible subset A⊆Ω; it occurs exactly when the realized outcome belongs to that subset.

An outcome and a singleton event have different types: ω is an element, whereas {ω} is a set. The expression P(ω) is common shorthand for P({ω}) when the singleton is measurable. This shorthand never turns the probability function into a function on arbitrary objects. The impossible event is ∅; the event that some permitted outcome occurs is Ω. Whether another event has probability zero or one requires the probability law, not just its set description.

For two distinguishable coin tosses, use Ω={HH,HT,TH,TT}, where the first symbol records the first toss. “At least one head” is {HH,HT,TH}; “exactly one head” is {HT,TH}. The outcome description contains no fairness assumption. The four outcomes have equal probabilities only under an additional model, such as two independent fair tosses. Independence itself will be defined and studied in the next chapter; here, a uniform assignment can simply be stated as the model's probability law.

2.2 Translating language into event algebra

Take complements relative to the declared Ω. For events A,B, the following translations determine the set before any probability formula is used.

Statement Event
Both occur A∩B
At least one occurs; inclusive “or” A∪B
Neither occurs (A∪B)c=Ac∩Bc
Exactly one occurs A△B=(A∖B)∪(B∖A)
The first occurs but the second does not A∖B=A∩Bc
They do not both occur (A∩B)c=Ac∪Bc
At least one of a family occurs ⋃iAi
Every event in a family occurs ⋂iAi

“Neither” and “not both” are different. On an outcome where only A occurs, “neither” is false but “not both” is true. “Mutually exclusive” means A∩B=∅; “exhaustive” means A∪B=Ω. Neither condition implies the other. A partition of a set is a family of nonempty, pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is that set. Partitions support exact addition because each outcome belongs to exactly one piece.

2.3 Granularity and the danger of assuming uniformity

Under a uniform four-outcome model for two coin tosses, record only the number of heads. The summary space is S={0,1,2}, but the masses are 1/4,1/2,1/4, not 1/3 each. The summary value one merges two detailed outcomes. In general, if a description map is g:Ω→S, then a summary event C⊆S receives probability

Q(C)=P(g−1(C)), where g−1(C)={ω∈Ω:g(ω)∈C}.

This is called the induced probability law. Only summary events whose preimages belong to the original event family are assigned probabilities. In the finite full-power-set example this requirement is automatic; in a general space it is the measurability requirement on the reporting map. Preimages preserve complements and countable unions, and disjoint summary events have disjoint preimages. These facts transfer normalization and countable additivity to the induced law.

If every detailed point has mass 1/N, the probability of a summary value is its number of detailed preimages divided by N. Summary values are equally likely exactly when those preimage sizes are equal. If two outcomes collapse to one summary value but an event distinguishes them, that event cannot be represented using the summary alone. The model must retain enough information for the question.

The process also matters. “Choose one of three devices uniformly” and “choose one of ten components uniformly, then report its device” need not give the same device probabilities. Similarly, unordered categories are not automatically equally likely simply because their names look symmetric. State the selection mechanism or the weights explicitly. A sequence tree lists possibilities and can preserve timing or stopping information, but its branch labels still require probabilities; the drawing does not generate a law by itself.

How to read the probability models

Outcome cards identify disjoint atoms. Their displayed masses are probabilities, while their rectangular areas are a layout choice unless an explicit quantitative scale is stated. Arrows in the reporting diagram merge detailed masses. In the conditional urn, gray pairs are excluded by the observation and surviving pairs share a new denominator. Bar heights in the collision and reporting models represent exact outcome counts.

A negative membership mass marks an impossible candidate law. Changing the triple mass while holding marginals fixed tests feasibility; it does not simulate independent events. Read the declared sampling mechanism before interpreting any animation.

3. Which subsets are events?

3.1 The event family and its closure rules

A probability space is a triple (Ω,𝓕,P). The set Ω describes outcomes; 𝓕 is a collection of subsets of Ω; and P assigns numbers to members of 𝓕. Thus A∈𝓕 and A⊆Ω are compatible statements at two different levels. The former says that A is an admissible event. The latter says it is made of outcomes.

The standard event family is a sigma-algebra (also called a sigma-field). It satisfies three conditions: Ω∈𝓕; if A∈𝓕, then Ac∈𝓕; and if A1,A2,…∈𝓕, then ⋃n≥1An∈𝓕. These closure requirements ensure that “not,” “at least one,” and their combinations remain questions to which the model assigns probabilities. “Countable” includes a finite family padded with empty sets.

The empty set belongs to 𝓕 because it is the complement of Ω. Countable intersections also belong: by De Morgan's identity, ⋂n≥1An=(⋃n≥1Anc)c. Complements, countable unions, and one final complement establish membership step by step. Differences and symmetric differences are consequently measurable too. An arbitrary uncountable union is not guaranteed by this definition; countable closure cannot be silently strengthened.

3.2 Finite spaces, partitions, and information

For a finite or countable Ω, taking 𝓕=2Ω, the power set, is a convenient standard choice. It is not compulsory. If Ω={1,2,3,4} but the only recorded question is “does the outcome belong to A={1,2}?”, the minimal event family that contains this question is {∅,A,Ac,Ω}. The event {1} is then unavailable: this observation cannot distinguish one from two.

A finite partition C1,…,Cr generates a sigma-algebra consisting of all unions of its cells. There are exactly 2r such unions because each nonempty cell is either selected or omitted, and distinct selections yield different sets. Complements omit precisely the selected cells; unions select every cell selected by at least one member. This proves closure directly. The cells are the indivisible atoms of this finite event family. They need not be singleton outcomes.

Assigning nonnegative cell masses q1,…,qr with sum one then defines a probability law on this coarse family: add the masses of selected cells. It does not specify how probability is distributed among individual outcomes inside a multi-outcome cell. A finer law requires additional information. This distinction explains why partial marginal probabilities can leave many models possible even when all supplied numbers are valid.

3.3 Continuous spaces and ordinary measurable sets

On [0,1], the standard Borel event family contains intervals and is closed under countable unions and complements. It therefore contains singletons, countable sets, and complements of countable sets. It is the smallest sigma-algebra containing the open sets relative to the interval. The familiar uniform law gives an interval its length. We use this established law here rather than construct it from scratch.

One should not claim that every subset of an uncountable space automatically has a probability under a chosen measure. There exist subsets for which a translation-invariant length assignment on all subsets cannot preserve the usual countably additive structure. Their construction is a separate measure-theory topic. For the ordinary intervals, regions, and countable operations used in this chapter, the events are measurable and the standard length/area model is sufficient. A set diagram alone still says nothing about density: its geometric area represents probability only when a uniform area law has actually been specified.

4. Axioms, exact identities, and feasibility

4.1 The countably additive probability law

On (Ω,𝓕), a probability law P:𝓕→ℝ satisfies nonnegativity, P(A)≥0 for each event; normalization, P(Ω)=1; and countable additivity: for pairwise disjoint events A1,A2,…,

P(⋃n≥1An)=∑n≥1P(An).

The infinite series is the limit of its nonnegative partial sums. It is not an axiom that probabilities add over overlapping events. Pairwise disjointness means every two different sets in the family have empty intersection; the weaker condition that the intersection of all the sets is empty is insufficient. Three sets can have an empty triple intersection while overlapping in pairs.

To derive P(∅)=0, apply countable additivity to the disjoint family Ω,∅,∅,…. Its union is Ω, so normalization gives 1=1+∑n≥1P(∅). Nonnegativity forces the repeated empty-set mass to be zero. Finite additivity now follows by padding any finite disjoint family with empty sets. This proof explains why the standard axioms include enough information for both finite and infinite calculations.

4.2 Complement, monotonicity, and the difference rule

Because A and Ac are disjoint and cover Ω, finite additivity gives P(A)+P(Ac)=1. Therefore P(Ac)=1−P(A). Since both terms are nonnegative, every event probability lies in [0,1]. The upper bound follows from the axioms; it need not be independently assumed.

If A⊆B, split B into disjoint sets A and B∖A. Thus P(B)=P(A)+P(B∖A)≥P(A), proving monotonicity and the exact difference rule P(B∖A)=P(B)−P(A) for nested events. For arbitrary events, the correct formula is P(A∖B)=P(A)−P(A∩B). Replacing the intersection with all of B is valid only when the relevant containment holds or the discarded portion has zero mass.

A proper subset can have the same probability as the larger event. Equality in monotonicity means P(B∖A)=0, not necessarily B∖A=∅. This distinction recurs in almost-sure statements and continuous models.

4.3 Inclusion-exclusion from disjoint pieces

The sets A∖B, A∩B, and B∖A partition A∪B after empty cells are omitted. Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice. Subtracting one copy yields

P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).

For three events, first add their individual masses, then subtract their three pairwise intersection masses, then add back the triple intersection. An outcome in all three was counted three times, subtracted three times, and must finally be counted once. An outcome in exactly two was counted twice and subtracted once. Thus

P(A∪B∪C)=P(A)+P(B)+P(C)
−P(A∩B)−P(A∩C)−P(B∩C)
+P(A∩B∩C).

For m events the general formula alternates over intersections of each possible size. Write [m]={1,…,m} and sum over nonempty index subsets J⊆[m]:

P(⋃i=1mAi)
=∑∅≠J⊆[m](−1)|J|+1P(⋂j∈JAj).

To verify the formula without assuming expectation theory, partition the sample space into the finitely many exact membership patterns of these events. On a cell belonging to exactly r≥1 events, its coefficient on the right is ∑k=1r(−1)k+1C(r,k)=1, by expanding (1−1)r=0. A cell belonging to none has coefficient zero. The weighted sum of these cell coefficients therefore equals the union's mass. The formula is finite; an unrestricted infinite alternating inclusion-exclusion expression requires extra convergence conditions and is not asserted here.

4.4 Union bounds through disjointification

For events that may overlap, remove everything already included: let D1=A1 and Dn=An∖⋃k<nAk. These events are pairwise disjoint, their union equals the original union, and Dn⊆An. Countable additivity and monotonicity now give the union bound:

P(⋃n≥1An)≤∑n≥1P(An).

No independence assumption is needed. A bound exceeding one remains algebraically true but can be improved to one and may provide little information. Applied to complements, the finite union bound gives P(⋂i=1mAi)≥1−∑i=1mP(Aic); combine this with zero if the right side is negative. If the sum of the probabilities of all bad events is strictly below one, their union has probability below one. Some outcome consequently avoids every bad event. This existence argument does not require constructing such an outcome.

For two events, equality P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B) holds precisely when P(A∩B)=0. Empty intersection is sufficient but not necessary. For a finite or countable family, pairwise zero-mass intersections likewise suffice because the overlaps removed during disjointification lie in countable unions of null events.

4.5 Four atomic masses and sharp feasibility bounds

Let a=P(A), b=P(B), and q=P(A∩B). The four membership regions have masses

Region Mass
Both q
First only a−q
Second only b−q
Neither 1−a−b+q

They sum to one. Nonnegativity of each region is equivalent, for a,b∈[0,1], to the Fréchet bounds

max(0,a+b−1) ≤ q ≤ min(a,b).

These bounds are necessary and sufficient. For any q in this interval, take four labelled outcomes representing the regions and assign the four listed masses. Their nonnegativity and unit total define a valid probability law. This explicit construction proves sharpness and prevents merely guessing whether supplied marginal numbers can coexist. It concerns consistency of an abstract two-event model; a specified physical mechanism may impose additional restrictions.

By substituting the permissible overlap interval into inclusion-exclusion, the union satisfies max(a,b)≤P(A∪B)≤min(1,a+b). Exactly one has probability P(A△B)=a+b−2q. It therefore obeys |a−b|≤P(A△B)≤min(a+b,2−a−b). Another useful stability inequality follows by writing P(A)−P(B)=P(A∖B)−P(B∖A) and applying the real-number inequality |u−v|≤u+v for nonnegative masses:

|P(A)−P(B)| ≤ P(A△B).

If the two events disagree only on a null set, their probabilities are equal. The reverse is false: equal probabilities do not imply that events coincide, even almost surely.

5. Constructing valid laws on different spaces

5.1 Finite and countable mass assignments

On finite Ω={ω1,…,ωN} with its full power set, assigning masses pi≥0 whose sum is one defines P(A)=∑ωi∈Api. Normalization is immediate; disjoint events select disjoint indices, so additivity follows. Conversely, the singleton events partition the finite space, forcing any probability law to have exactly this representation. Negative mass cannot be repaired by arranging other positive masses to sum to one.

When all masses are equal, normalization gives pi=1/N and P(A)=|A|/N. This count ratio is a theorem for a finite uniform law. A “random” choice without an explicit mechanism does not prove uniformity. The phrase should be clarified by a symmetry assumption, a stated sampling rule, or supplied weights.

On Ω={1,2,…}, a nonnegative sequence with ∑n≥1pn=1 similarly defines a law on all subsets by summing their singleton masses. Countable additivity follows from regrouping a nonnegative series over disjoint index sets. Unlike a conditionally convergent signed series, such a series has no order-dependent sum. As an example, pn=1/[n(n+1)] works because 1/[n(n+1)]=1/n−1/(n+1) and its first m terms sum to 1−1/(m+1)→1.

There is no uniform countably additive probability law on the positive integers that gives each singleton the same mass. If that mass is c>0, sufficiently many points have total mass mc>1; if it is zero, countable additivity makes the entire space have mass zero. Both possibilities contradict normalization. An “equal chance of any positive integer” is therefore an invalid assumption in this standard model.

5.2 Uniform length and area

For a uniform choice on [u,v] with u<v, ordinary subintervals have probability equal to their length divided by v−u. A singleton has probability zero: it is contained in intervals of arbitrarily small length, so monotonicity bounds its mass by quantities approaching zero. Thus open or closed endpoints do not alter an interval's probability under this law. They still alter the event as a set.

For a uniform point in the unit square, probability is area because the total area is one. The event x+y≤t for 0≤t≤1 is a right triangle with legs t, giving probability t2/2. For 1≤t≤2, its complement is a right triangle near (1,1) with legs 2−t, giving probability 1−(2−t)2/2. Thresholds below zero have probability zero; thresholds at least two have probability one. No count ratio between infinite cardinalities is used.

5.3 Null events, almost sure events, and mixed laws

The implication A=∅⇒P(A)=0 is always true; its converse is not. A specified point in a uniform interval is a nonempty event of probability zero. Similarly, P(A)=1 means almost sure, not necessarily A=Ω. In a uniform [0,1] model, (0,1] is a proper subset with probability one. In a finite model where every singleton has strictly positive mass, null events are empty; allowing zero-mass singleton outcomes removes that implication even in a finite space.

A countable union of null events is null by the union bound. In particular, the rational points in [0,1] have probability zero under a uniform law, and an irrational outcome has probability one. An uncountable union of null singletons can instead be the whole interval of probability one. Countable additivity says nothing about an uncountable sum of singleton masses.

Zero mass for every singleton is also not universal for an uncountable sample space. On [0,1], put mass α∈[0,1] at zero and spread the remaining 1−α uniformly over the interval. For a Borel event, define P(A)=α·1{0∈A}+(1−α)λ(A), where λ is the unit-interval length law. This is a convex combination of two probability measures, so normalization and countable additivity hold term by term. The point zero now has mass α. The sample space alone does not tell us whether a law is discrete, continuous, or mixed.

6. Countable event sequences and their limits

6.1 Continuity from below

Suppose A1⊆A2⊆⋯. Define disjoint increments D1=A1 and Dn=An∖An−1. Their first m members partition Am, and all their members cover ⋃n≥1An. Consequently,

P(Am)=∑n=1mP(Dn),
P(⋃n≥1An)=limm→∞P(Am).

The second equality is the defining limit of a nonnegative series together with countable additivity. It is called continuity from below. It is continuity along increasing events, not continuity of an arbitrary set-valued function. For uniform [0,1], the events [0,1−1/n] increase to [0,1) and their probabilities approach one. The union remains a proper subset of the original interval.

6.2 Continuity from above

If A1⊇A2⊇⋯, their complements increase. Apply continuity from below to those complements and use De Morgan's identity and the complement rule:

P(⋂n≥1An)
=1−P(⋃n≥1Anc)
=1−limn→∞P(Anc)
=limn→∞P(An).

The total measure is finite because it is a probability law, so the subtraction from one is valid. For general measures with infinite total mass, continuity from above requires an additional finite-mass condition and cannot be transferred automatically. In uniform [0,1], [0,1/n] decreases to {0}. Its probabilities approach zero while its limiting event is nonempty.

6.3 Infinitely often versus eventually always

An arbitrary sequence need not have a single monotone set limit. Two useful events remain well-defined:

limsup An=⋂m≥1⋃n≥mAn (infinitely often),
liminf An=⋃m≥1⋂n≥mAn (eventually always).

An outcome belongs to the first if every tail contains at least one occurrence; it belongs to the second if some tail contains only occurrences. These definitions use only countable unions and intersections, so both are measurable. “Eventually always” implies “infinitely often,” hence liminf An⊆limsup An.

For a detailed proof, write Bm=⋂n≥mAn and Cm=⋃n≥mAn. The first sequence increases and the second decreases. For every n≥m, inclusion gives P(Bm)≤P(An)≤P(Cm). Therefore the first quantity is at most the infimum of the numerical tail, while the last is at least its supremum. Let m tend to infinity. Monotone continuity identifies the limits of the event probabilities as the probabilities of the liminf and limsup events. The definitions of numerical liminf and limsup identify the limits of the tail infima and suprema. This proves

P(liminf An)≤liminf P(An)
≤limsup P(An)≤P(limsup An).

These are inequalities, not unrestricted equalities. Even P(An)→0 does not force the probability of infinitely many occurrences to be zero. At successive levels, enumerate every half-open dyadic cell partitioning [0,1). At level k, each cell has mass 2−k; those masses tend to zero as the cells are enumerated. Yet every point lies in one cell at every level and hence belongs to infinitely many of the events. The limsup is [0,1), an event of probability one; if the ambient space is [0,1], the endpoint 1 is still excluded. This is almost-sure occurrence, not equality with the entire closed sample space. This counterexample rules out a tempting but invalid limit interchange.

6.4 A summable-error consequence

Suppose instead that ∑n≥1P(An)<∞. The union bound gives P(⋃n≥mAn)≤∑n≥mP(An). The tail of a convergent nonnegative series tends to zero. The tail unions decrease to the infinitely-often event, so continuity from above yields P(limsup An)=0. This is the first Borel–Cantelli implication, derived here directly from the axioms. It requires no independence. Divergence of the sum does not reverse the conclusion: taking every event to be the same event of probability 1/2 gives a divergent sum but an infinitely-often probability of only 1/2. Further converse results need additional hypotheses and belong to later probability study.

7. Interactive laboratory: four regions, one probability law

Two event probabilities do not determine their overlap. This laboratory displays the four disjoint regions underlying every pair of events. Change the two marginal probabilities and their proposed overlap. A negative region makes the proposal impossible; a valid proposal supplies an explicit probability model. No independence assumption is made.

Explore the overlap constraint

Values are percentages. The starting model has event probabilities 65% and 45%, with 25% overlap.

The display represents probability mass, not necessarily geometric area in the original experiment. A valid four-region model proves feasibility of these three probabilities; it does not establish that a particular physical experiment actually follows that law. Use the calculation to inspect assumptions, not to invent observations.

Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

Recover all four atomic probabilities

Given P(A)=a, P(B)=b and P(A∩B)=t, the four disjoint masses are t,a-t,b-t,1-a-b+t. Nonnegativity yields max(0,a+b-1)≤t≤min(a,b). This inequality is both necessary and sufficient: if it holds, the four numbers define a valid law on four atoms. Thus feasibility questions can be solved without guessing independence.

The union is a+b-t, exactly one is a+b-2t, neither is 1-a-b+t, and A without B is a-t. These are distinct events. A diagram of the four regions determines the coefficient of t and is safer than memorizing ambiguous phrases such as “either.” When the question says “either but not both,” it means symmetric difference.

A count ratio requires equally likely elementary outcomes

If a fair die's outcomes are grouped into parity, the two groups are equally likely because each contains three equally likely faces. Grouping into “one” versus “not one” creates masses 16 and 56, not 12 each. For a nonuniform finite law, sum the masses of favorable elementary outcomes. A probability density at a point is not its point probability.

Infinite sums and limiting events

For a countable discrete law pk=c/2k for k≥1, normalization uses the convergent geometric series and gives c=1. For a uniform point on [0,1], an interval's mass is its length while every singleton has probability zero. Countable unions of null singletons remain null, but the uncountable union of every singleton is the whole interval. Countable additivity deliberately does not extend to arbitrary uncountable sums.

For increasing measurable events, P(⋃An)=limP(An); for decreasing ones, P(⋂An)=limP(An) in a probability space. A moving interval sequence can have empty intersection even when each individual interval has positive mass. “Infinitely often” is an intersection of tail unions, while “eventually always” is a union of tail intersections.

Detailed derivation tutorials

The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

The problems below are original formulations. Their instructional targets synthesize the reviewed courses: MIT and Stanford inform finite experiment modeling; Berkeley and ETH inform measurable events, axioms, and limits; Oxford informs union-bound reasoning. None is represented as a verbatim university examination question. The foundational tutorials below precede the independently labeled examination applications. Additional counting, conditional-probability and moment tools needed by that bank are derived in the mathematical constructions section. Each solution makes its model explicit before using a formula.

Tutorial 1. Translate a verbal event before calculating

Two independent fair coins are tossed in order. Let A mean that the first coin is heads and B mean that the second is heads. Find the probabilities of “at least one head,” “exactly one head,” and “the first is heads but the second is not.”

Solution. The ordered space is Ω={HH,HT,TH,TT}, and the stated fair independent model assigns mass 1/4 to every outcome. Thus A={HH,HT} and B={HH,TH}. “At least one” is the union {HH,HT,TH}, with mass 3/4. “Exactly one” is the symmetric difference {HT,TH}, with mass 1/2. “First but not second” is A∖B={HT}, with mass 1/4.

The union includes the two-head outcome, whereas the symmetric difference excludes it. Treating the word “or” as “exactly one” changes the event and therefore the answer. The probabilities used here come from the stated law; the list of four outcomes alone would not imply equal masses.

Tutorial 2. A smaller sample space need not be uniform

In Problem 1, retain only the number of heads. A proposed answer says that the three possible results 0, 1, and 2 each have probability 1/3. Diagnose and repair it.

Solution. The reporting map sends TT to 0, HT and TH to 1, and HH to 2. The probability of a reported value equals the sum of the masses of its preimages. Consequently,

Q({0})=1/4, Q({1})=1/2, Q({2})=1/4.

The map merges two elementary outcomes for the middle category and one for each other category. It does not create a new randomization mechanism. The repaired model gives Q({1,2})=3/4, agreeing with the ordered model. The incorrect uniform model gives 2/3. A valid change of representation preserves the probabilities of corresponding events; it need not preserve equal likelihood of the newly named outcomes.

Tutorial 3. Normalize a weighted finite law

Four outcomes have masses k,2k,3k,4k. Determine k and the probability of the event containing the second and fourth outcomes. Explain why normalization alone would not suffice for arbitrary proposed weights.

Solution. The total mass is 10k, so normalization forces k=1/10. All four masses are then nonnegative. On the full power set, assigning an event the sum of its singleton masses gives a probability law: disjoint events collect disjoint summands, and the total is one. The requested probability is 2k+4k=3/5.

A collection such as (0.6,0.6,−0.2) sums to one but cannot be a probability law because one singleton has negative mass. Always check both nonnegativity and normalization. For a countably infinite space, also verify the infinite series rather than merely a finite partial sum.

Tutorial 4. Test a proposed event collection

Let Ω={1,2,3,4}. A proposed event collection contains only the empty set, Ω, and {1,2},{3,4},{1,3},{2,4}. Is it a sigma-algebra? What sigma-algebra do these sets generate?

Solution. The collection contains complements, but this is only one closure requirement. The intersection of {1,2} and {1,3} is {1}, which is missing. Closure under complements and unions would imply closure under intersections by De Morgan's identity, so the collection fails. Its union {1,2,3} is another missing event.

To find the generated collection, intersect each of the two crossing sets or its complement. The resulting four regions are the four singletons. Every subset of Ω is a union of these singletons, so the generated sigma-algebra is the full power set, containing 24=16 events. This argument identifies the information atoms before counting their possible unions.

Tutorial 5. A coarse event collection hides singleton probabilities

Suppose the only events are ∅,Ω,{1,2},{3,4}, and the first pair has probability 0.3. Can the probability of {1} be recovered?

Solution. The stated collection is a sigma-algebra generated by a two-cell partition. Normalization assigns mass 0.7 to the second cell. The singleton {1} is not an event of this probability space, so its probability is not defined by this law.

Even if we choose to extend the law to all subsets, uniqueness fails. The singleton masses (0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4) and (0.25,0.05,0.6,0.1) both reproduce the two stated cell masses but disagree on the requested singleton. Indeed any first mass in [0,0.3] can be paired with the remaining mass in the first cell. An undefined probability is different from a probability that happens to be zero.

Tutorial 6. Recover overlap and one-sided differences

Given P(A)=0.55, P(B)=0.40, and P(A∪B)=0.70, find the overlap, A only, B only, and neither. Check that the data define a possible model.

Solution. Inclusion–exclusion gives overlap 0.55+0.40−0.70=0.25. Subtract it from each marginal: A only has mass 0.30 and B only has mass 0.15. The complement of the union has mass 0.30. The four masses are 0.25,0.30,0.15,0.30; all are nonnegative and their sum is one.

Assign these masses to four elementary outcomes labeled both, A only, B only, and neither. The events A and B formed from these labels have exactly the supplied probabilities. This establishes feasibility, rather than merely producing algebraic answers. Notice that A only is a difference event; it is not the complement of B, which also includes neither.

Tutorial 7. Detect an impossible proposed overlap

Can two events satisfy P(A)=0.7, P(B)=0.6, and P(A∩B)=0.2?

Solution. The implied union probability is 0.7+0.6−0.2=1.1, exceeding one. Equivalently, the neither region has mass 1−0.7−0.6+0.2=−0.1. Both contradictions come from the same four-region partition.

For these marginals the admissible overlap interval is [max(0,0.7+0.6−1),min(0.7,0.6)]=[0.3,0.6]. Every value in this interval is realizable by the four-region construction. The upper bound alone would not detect the proposed error; the lower bound is essential when the marginals sum to more than one.

Tutorial 8. Find sharp bounds without assuming dependence

Only P(A)=0.4 and P(B)=0.5 are known. Find the smallest and largest possible union probabilities, and construct laws attaining them.

Solution. The overlap can range from zero to 0.4. Since union mass is 0.9−q, the union lies in [0.5,0.9]. For the lower endpoint take the four masses in the order both, A only, B only, neither to be (0.4,0,0.1,0.5). Here A lies inside B up to a null region. For the upper endpoint use (0,0.4,0.5,0.1); here the two positive-mass regions are disjoint.

The constructions prove that neither bound can be improved from the marginals alone. Multiplying the marginals to set overlap to 0.2 would impose an additional independence assumption and give just one admissible model, not the sharp range.

Tutorial 9. Distinguish exclusive and inclusive alternatives

Let P(A)=0.65, P(B)=0.45, and overlap be 0.25. Find exactly one, at least one, neither, and the probability that A fails while B occurs.

Solution. The region masses are both 0.25, A only 0.40, B only 0.20, and neither 0.15. Exactly one therefore has mass 0.40+0.20=0.60. At least one also includes both and has mass 0.85. Neither is 0.15. The last event is B only and has mass 0.20.

The symmetric-difference formula yields the same first answer: 0.65+0.45−2(0.25)=0.60. Two copies of overlap must be removed because neither occurrence of the intersection belongs to “exactly one.” In contrast, the union subtracts overlap once because it should retain one copy.

Tutorial 10. Audit three-event inclusion–exclusion

Three events have eight membership-region masses as follows. Calculate each marginal, the union, exactly one occurrence, exactly two occurrences, and at least two occurrences.

Membership region Mass
None 0.05
A only 0.10
B only 0.15
C only 0.20
A and B only 0.10
A and C only 0.15
B and C only 0.05
All three 0.20

Solution. The listed masses sum to one and are nonnegative. Add the rows containing each event: P(A)=0.55, P(B)=0.50, and P(C)=0.60. Pairwise intersections include the last row, so their probabilities are 0.30, 0.35, and 0.25, respectively. Inclusion–exclusion gives

P(A∪B∪C)=0.55+0.50+0.60−0.30−0.35−0.25+0.20=0.95.

This agrees with one minus the none row. Exactly one is 0.10+0.15+0.20=0.45. Exactly two is 0.10+0.15+0.05=0.30, and at least two is 0.30+0.20=0.50. Adding pairwise-intersection probabilities gives 0.90, which counts the triple region three times and is not the probability of either of these last events.

Tutorial 11. Pairwise feasibility does not establish joint feasibility

Suppose three events each have probability 0.5, and every pairwise intersection has probability zero. Each pair satisfies its two-event overlap bounds. Can all three conditions hold together?

Solution. The triple intersection is contained in every pairwise intersection and therefore also has probability zero. Inclusion–exclusion forces the union probability to be 0.5+0.5+0.5=1.5, a contradiction. Equivalently, removing the null overlaps leaves three disjoint positive-mass regions whose masses already exceed the total mass.

The pairwise overlap interval for two marginals 0.5 is [0,0.5], so each individual pair passes. Their three simultaneous constraints do not. For three or more events, write all membership regions or additional joint constraints; pairwise checks are necessary but not sufficient.

Tutorial 12. Reliability bounds with unknown dependence

Three possible faults have probabilities at most 0.01, 0.02, and 0.03. No dependence information is available. What guaranteed lower bound follows for no fault? Can a product formula be used?

Solution. The event of at least one fault is the union of the three fault events. The union bound gives probability at most 0.01+0.02+0.03=0.06. Taking its complement gives no-fault probability at least 0.94.

This guarantee remains valid whether faults tend to occur together or separately. A product of three success probabilities would require independence and exact marginal values; neither is supplied. The bound is attainable when the three fault events are disjoint with the stated masses and the remaining 0.94 is assigned to no fault. If a sum of fault bounds exceeds one, cap the union bound at one and the resulting success lower bound at zero.

Tutorial 13. Work with a mixed continuous and atomic law

On [0,1], place mass 2/5 at zero and distribute the rest uniformly. Find the probabilities of {0}, (0,1/2], [0,1/2], and the rational points in the interval.

Solution. Apply the mixed-law formula to each event. The singleton zero receives the atomic mass 2/5; its length is zero. The half-open interval excludes the atom and has length 1/2, so its mass is (3/5)(1/2)=3/10. The closed half-interval includes the atom, so its mass is 2/5+3/10=7/10.

The rational points are a countable Borel set of length zero, but contain zero. Their total mass is therefore 2/5, not zero. The irrational points carry the remaining 3/5. A countable set is null under this uniform component; countability alone does not make it null under every probability law.

Tutorial 14. Normalize a telescoping countable law

On the positive integers, set pn=1/[n(n+1)]. Prove that these weights define a law and find the probability of an outcome at least m.

Solution. Every weight is nonnegative. Rewrite it as 1/n−1/(n+1). The first N weights sum to 1−1/(N+1), whose limit is one. Thus assigning each subset the sum of its weights gives a normalized countably additive law.

For integers N≥m≥1, the finite tail sum is 1/m−1/(N+1). Taking N to infinity gives P({m,m+1,…})=1/m. In particular, P({1,2,3})=1−1/4=3/4. The calculation depends on the infinite-series limit, not on treating the positive integers as equiprobable.

Tutorial 15. Separate odd and even outcomes in a countable model

Let pn=2/3n for n≥1. Verify normalization, then calculate even-outcome probability and the tail probability from m onward.

Solution. The geometric sum is 2(1/3)/(1−1/3)=1. Even outcomes have indices n=2k, so their total mass is 2∑k≥1(1/9)k=2(1/9)/(1−1/9)=1/4. The complement gives odd-outcome probability 3/4.

Factoring the first term out of the tail yields ∑n≥m2/3n=(2/3ᵐ)/(1−1/3)=31−m. The even and odd sets have the same countably infinite cardinality but unequal probability. Cardinality ratios cannot replace weighted sums in an infinite probability model.

Tutorial 16. Prove that uniform positive-integer sampling is impossible

A model claims to select each positive integer with the same probability c. Show that no countably additive probability law on all subsets can satisfy this claim.

Solution. Nonnegativity requires c≥0. If c>0, choose a finite number N with Nc>1. Finite additivity makes the first N integers have probability Nc, contradicting the upper bound one. Therefore c must be zero. Countable additivity would then assign the union of all singleton integers probability ∑0=0, contradicting normalization.

These two cases exhaust the possible common masses. A uniform draw from the finite set {1,…,N} is valid for each N, but those finite laws do not justify a uniform law on the entire positive-integer space. The failure is a property of the proposed law, not a prohibition on nonuniform countable laws.

Tutorial 17. Compute a continuous probability by area

A point is uniform in the unit square. Find the probability that its coordinates sum to at most 3/2. Why is this an area calculation rather than a count of favorable points?

Solution. The excluded region satisfies x+y>3/2. Inside the square it is the corner triangle with vertices (1/2,1),(1,1/2),(1,1). Its two perpendicular legs each have length 1/2, so its area is (1/2)(1/2)(1/2)=1/8. The desired probability is 1−1/8=7/8.

The line boundary has area zero, so including it does not change this probability under the specified area law. Both the favorable set and the square contain uncountably many points; dividing their cardinalities is not the definition of this law. The uniform-area assumption is the reason that geometric area gives probability.

Tutorial 18. Distinguish impossible from null, and certain from exhaustive

On Ω={u,v,w}, assign masses (1/2,1/2,0). Give a nonempty null event and a proper event with probability one. How does the answer change if every singleton has positive mass?

Solution. The event {w} is nonempty but has probability zero. The event {u,v} is proper because it omits w, yet has probability one. Normalization concerns total mass; it does not require every named outcome to carry positive mass.

If every singleton in a finite space has positive mass, any nonempty event contains at least one positive-mass singleton, so it has positive probability by monotonicity. A proper event then has a nonempty complement of positive mass, making its own probability less than one. The extra strict-positivity assumption is indispensable. It cannot be extended to uniform continuous laws, where individual points have mass zero.

Tutorial 19. Add events whose overlap is nonempty but null

Under the uniform law on [0,1], take A=[0,1/2] and B=[1/2,1]. They are not disjoint. Is adding their probabilities nonetheless correct?

Solution. Each interval has mass 1/2. Their intersection is the singleton {1/2}, which is nonempty but has mass zero. Inclusion–exclusion therefore gives union probability 1/2+1/2−0=1.

Disjointness is a sufficient set-theoretic condition for adding two event probabilities. The more general numerical condition is a zero-probability intersection. Do not reverse the implication: equality of the union probability and the sum does not force the intersection to be empty. If the model placed positive atomic mass at the shared endpoint, the subtraction would become essential.

Tutorial 20. Equal event probabilities do not mean equal events

On four equally likely outcomes, let A={1,2} and B={3,4}. Evaluate both sides of |P(A)−P(B)|≤P(A△B), then explain when the right side being zero is informative.

Solution. Both probabilities are 1/2, so the left side is zero. The events are disjoint and their symmetric difference is the entire space, so the right side is one. Equal probabilities carry very little information about agreement of events.

Conversely, if P(A△B)=0, the two one-sided differences are null. They therefore have equal probabilities and agree outside a null set. They need not be literally equal: two continuous events can differ by one endpoint. The inequality follows by subtracting the two difference-region masses and using |x−y|≤x+y for nonnegative x and y.

Tutorial 21. Find an increasing union without adding its overlap repeatedly

For a uniform point on [0,1], let An=[0,1−1/n]. Find the union and its probability. Explain why summing the individual probabilities fails.

Solution. The events increase. Every point less than one eventually belongs because an integer n can be chosen with 1/n≤1−x. The endpoint one never belongs. Thus the union is [0,1), whose mass is one. Continuity from below gives the same result from P(An)=1−1/n→1.

These events are nested, not disjoint. Their probabilities cannot be added; that series diverges. To use countable additivity directly, split the union into the initial event and consecutive difference events. Those disjoint increments telescope to the limit of the original probabilities. This is why monotone continuity and countable additivity are compatible.

Tutorial 22. A decreasing limit retains an atom

In the mixed law with atomic mass α at zero, let An=[0,1/n]. Find each probability and the probability of the intersection. Compare with the purely uniform case.

Solution. Every interval includes the atom and has length 1/n. Therefore P(An)=α+(1−α)/n. The events decrease to {0}: zero belongs to all of them, while any positive point is excluded once n is sufficiently large. Continuity from above gives the limit α, exactly the atom's mass.

For α=0, the limit is zero although the intersection is nonempty. For α=1, every interval and its singleton intersection have mass one. The same sequence of sets exhibits different probabilities under different laws. Set geometry cannot determine probability without a specified measure.

Tutorial 23. Bound all future failures using a summable tail

Failure events satisfy P(An)≤2−n−2 for all n≥1. Bound the probability of any failure from step m onward, and determine an m making that bound at most 0.001. What follows about infinitely many failures?

Solution. Countable union bounding and a geometric tail give

P(⋃n≥mAn)≤∑n≥m2−n−2=2−m−1.

For m equal to 9, the bound is 1/1024≈0.0009765625, at most 0.001. For m equal to 8 it is 1/512≈0.001953125, so 9 is the smallest integer justified by this bound.

The tail union events decrease as m increases, and their probabilities tend to zero. Their intersection is the event of infinitely many failures. Continuity from above therefore makes that event null. This argument requires no independence. It gives an almost sure statement, rather than a claim that every mathematical outcome has only finitely many failures.

Tutorial 24. Vanishing probabilities can still occur infinitely often

Partition [0,1) into half-open intervals of length 2-k for each level k=1,2,…. Enumerate all cells at level 1, then all at level 2, and so on, using each cell as the next event. Under the uniform length law, find the limiting individual probabilities, the infinitely-often event, and the eventually-always event.

Solution. There are finitely many cells at each level. Hence an index tending to infinity eventually passes every fixed level, and its level tends to infinity. Each event at level k has probability 2-k, so the individual event probabilities tend to zero.

Each point belongs to exactly one cell at every level, including dyadic boundary points because the cells are half-open. It therefore belongs to infinitely many enumerated events. The infinitely-often event is the whole sample space, with probability one. At every level there are also cells omitting that point; after any proposed starting index, a later level supplies such an omission. No point is in all events of a tail. The eventually-always event is empty, with probability zero.

At each level the sum of the probabilities of its cells is one, so the series of all event probabilities diverges. There is no contradiction with the summable-error theorem. The example shows exactly why a limit of individual probabilities cannot be substituted for the probability of a limsup event.

Mathematical constructions for the revised question bank

1. Recover an entire two-event law before computing a target

Given a=P(A), b=P(B) and u=P(A∪B), recover q=a+b-u. The four masses in order both, first only, second only, neither are q,a-q,b-q,1-u. A tuple can have each supplied number in [0,1] and still be impossible: for example a=4/5,b=7/10,u=1/2 implies a-q=-1/5. Check every atomic mass, not just normalization.

With only a,b known, all possible overlaps satisfy max(0,a+b-1)≤q≤min(a,b). Necessity follows from the four nonnegative masses. Sufficiency follows by constructing a four-point space carrying those masses. Because exactly one has probability a+b-2q, its sharp range is |a-b|≤P(A△B)≤min(a+b,2-a-b). The coefficient minus two makes this target decrease as overlap increases. A proof of a bound must show why no model can exceed it and supply a model attaining the claimed endpoint.

2. Invert a three-event table and prove feasibility constructively

Write a,b,c for marginals; d,e,f for AB,AC,BC intersections; and t for the triple. The exact atoms are

t,d-t,e-t,f-t,a-d-e+t,b-d-f+t,c-e-f+t,1-a-b-c+d+e+f-t.

Their eight nonnegativity inequalities reduce to

max(0,d+e-a,d+f-b,e+f-c)≤t≤min(d,e,f,1-a-b-c+d+e+f).

If the lower endpoint exceeds the upper, no probability law realizes the given data. Otherwise, placing these masses on eight binary membership strings constructs every permissible value of t. Summing the strings with first bit one recovers a; summing those with first two bits one recovers d. This verifies sufficiency without imposing independence. In a physical model, additional mechanism constraints may narrow the abstract interval. The checkpoint model displays the actual atoms and their total rather than drawing overlapping circles whose areas might misleadingly suggest prescribed masses.

3. Change descriptions by preimages and conditioning by renormalization

A reporting map g:Ω→S induces Q(C)=P(g-1(C)). It merges masses of detailed outcomes. In a finite uniform space, the mass of a reported value is its fiber size divided by |Ω|; a uniform input need not induce a uniform report. Preimages preserve complements and disjoint unions, so the induced law preserves the probability axioms whenever the relevant preimages are measurable.

Conditioning on an event H with positive mass instead restricts outcomes to H and uses PH(E)=P(E∩H)/P(H). For disjoint Ei, the intersections Ei∩H remain disjoint, so division by the fixed positive denominator preserves additivity. The conditioned space has total mass P(H)/P(H)=1. In a finite uniform model, its surviving detailed points remain uniform, but coarser categories still require their inherited weights. A probability-zero condition cannot be handled by this division; later continuous conditioning needs additional definitions, not division by zero.

4. Derive product-model and indicator tools needed by the archived questions

For independent binary coordinates with success probabilities pi, assign a binary pattern s mass ∏ipisi(1-pi)1-si. Summing over all patterns gives ∏i(pi+(1-pi))=1. Fixing some coordinates and summing over the others proves the needed subset products. This construction explains which independence premise supports a many-event multiplication; pairwise products alone do not specify every pattern.

If K=∑iIi, exactly zero uses the all-zero pattern, and exactly one is a disjoint sum over its unique successful index. Expectations require a different argument: in a finite model, interchange finite sums in E[K]=∑ωP(ω)∑iIi(ω) to obtain ∑iE[Ii], with no independence requirement. Expand the square to obtain the variance identity with all covariances. Pairwise independence suffices for those second-order products, although it does not suffice for an arbitrary-length all-failure product. These tools are included here to make the existing authentic applications self-contained; their systematic theory continues in the later counting, conditional-probability and random-variable chapters.

5. Distinguish exact unions, bounds and higher-order overlap corrections

For three events, the sum of marginals counts an outcome belonging to r events exactly r times. Subtracting the three pair intersections removes (r2) copies; adding the triple restores (r3). For r=1,2,3, the final coefficient is always one. This outcome-wise coefficient calculation proves inclusion-exclusion on arbitrary weighted atoms, not only on uniform outcomes.

The union bound retains the initial nonnegative overcount, so it needs no independence. Its gap for a finite family equals E[K]-P(K≥1)=E[(K-1)1{K≥1}], where K is the number of occurring events. Thus the gap vanishes precisely when multiple occurrence has probability zero. In the three-label collision problem, exactly one repeated pair contributes no gap, while each all-equal outcome contributes two extra counts. A bound of one does not prove certainty; it may simply be the point at which the numerical upper bound becomes uninformative.

6. Separate monotone event limits from numerical limits

If An increases, disjoint increments D1=A1 and Dn=An∖An-1 partition each stage. Countable additivity identifies the limiting partial sum with P(⋃nAn). Decreasing continuity follows by taking complements; probability measures have finite total mass, so subtraction is legitimate. These are proofs about nested sets in one fixed space.

For arbitrary events, the infinitely-often event is ⋂m⋃n≥mAn, whereas eventual permanent occurrence is ⋃m⋂n≥mAn. A moving dyadic interval can have probability tending to zero while almost every point belongs to infinitely many intervals. A stronger summability condition ∑nP(An)<∞ makes each tail union at most the numerical series tail, forcing infinitely-often probability zero by decreasing continuity. Every use of a limit must identify the sets and the applicable theorem; numerical convergence alone is not a set-limit theorem.

Formula and conceptual problem bank

This bank combines authentic Iranian entrance-examination questions, newly authored medium/hard analogues, and two retained multistep challenges. The original four-option numbering is retained for authentic questions. Difficulty labels for original problems are qualitative author judgments, not calibrated response statistics.

Authentic examinations · Original analogues · Integrated challenges

Authentic examination questions

Question 1. PhD CS 1405, Q21 — Minimum count outside three sets

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 21. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Thirty-two offices each have a computer. Fifteen have a laser printer, ten have a scanner, eight have a modem, and two have all three. What is the minimum number with none of these three devices?

1.

1

2.

2

3.

3

4.

4

Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 3. Count offices, not memberships. Let the three device sets be A,B,C, and let s be the number of offices belonging to exactly two sets. The two offices in all three sets contribute six memberships while using only two offices. Each pair-only office contributes one additional duplicated membership. Therefore

|A∪B∪C|=15+10+8-2·2-s=29-s.

The outside count is consequently 32-(29-s)=3+s. Because s≥0, at least three offices must have no device. A lower bound is not yet a minimum: exhibit a configuration attaining it.

Exact membership Number of offices
All three 2
Printer only 13
Scanner only 8
Modem only 6
Exactly two 0
None 3

The table totals 32 and reproduces all three marginals: 13+2=15, 8+2=10, 6+2=8. Thus the lower bound is attainable. Options one and two would require negative s. Four is possible with s=1, but it is not the minimum. If using inclusion-exclusion, remember that each pair intersection already includes both triple offices; their compulsory contribution totals six, followed by adding back two, for a net four duplicated memberships removed.

Question 2. PhD CS 1404, Q68 — At most one independent event

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 15 · question 68. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Events B1,…,Bn are independent, and P(Bi)=1/n. What is the probability that at most one occurs? Take n≥2 in the displayed formulas.

1.
(n-1)n-1(2n-1)nn
2.
nn-1(2n-1)(n+1)n
3.
(n/(n-1))n
4.
((n-1)/(n+1))n
Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 1. Let K count the occurring events. “At most one” is the disjoint union of K=0 and K=1. Write p=1/n and q=1-p, with n≥2. Mutual independence includes the needed complements, so the all-failure event has probability qn.

For a specified unique index i, the event Bi∩⋂j≠iBjc has probability pqn-1. These n events are disjoint: two different indices cannot both be the unique success. Consequently

P(K≤1)=qn+npqn-1=qn-1(q+1)=(n-1)n-1(2n-1)nn.

At n=2, the only excluded outcome is two successes, so the result must be 1-1/4=3/4, agreeing with option one. Option two evaluates to 2/3, option three to four, and option four to 1/9; the value four is immediately impossible for a probability. At general n, replacing the failure probability by (n-1)/(n+1) changes the specified model. As n grows, the result approaches 2/e, since qn-1→e-1 and q+1→2. For the omitted endpoint n=1, the sole event occurs certainly and the answer is one; compute this case directly rather than interpret 00 implicitly. Pairwise independence alone does not supply all the products used above.

Question 3. PhD CS 1404, Q69 — A conditional probability with random family size

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 15 · question 69. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

The probability that a family has n children is 2-n-1 for n≥0. Independently, each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl. Given that the family has no boys, what is the probability it has at least one child?

1.

1/3

2.

1/2

3.

3/4

4.

1/4

Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 4. Let N be family size, G the event of no boys, and H={N≥1}. The prior masses P(N=n)=2-n-1 sum to one, beginning with P(N=0)=1/2. A childless family satisfies G: it has no boy. Given size n, independent fair genders give P(G∣N=n)=2-n, including value one at zero.

The size classes partition the sample space, so add their joint contributions:

P(G)=∑n=0∞2-n-12-n=12∑n=0∞4-n=23.
Size contribution Prior mass Joint mass with no boys
Zero 1/2 1/2
One 1/4 1/8
Two 1/8 1/32
All sizes at least one 1/2 1/6

Subtract only the zero-size joint mass: P(G∩H)=2/3-1/2=1/6. Conditioning renormalizes by the full mass of G, not by the mass of H:

P(H∣G)=1/62/3=14.

Option one is the reversed conditional P(G∣H)=(1/6)/(1/2)=1/3. Option two is the unconditional P(H)=1/2. Three quarters is the conditional probability of being childless given no boys, P(Hc∣G)=(1/2)/(2/3). These are valid probabilities of different events, which is precisely why preserving the conditioning direction matters. Removing childless families before computing the denominator changes the question.

Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q70 — Equal heads from unequal sample sizes

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 70. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Player A tosses a fair coin 25 times and player B tosses a fair coin 20 times, independently. What is the probability that they obtain the same number of heads?

1.
(4520)2-45
2.
(4515)2-45
3.
(4520)2-20
4.
(4515)2-20
Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 1. Model all 45 tosses as independent fair binary outcomes. The detailed space has 245 equally likely elements. If both players obtain k heads, the first player has (25k) possible sequences and the second has (20k), with 0≤k≤20. The values of k identify disjoint cases, giving

P(equal heads)=2-45∑k=020(25k)(20k).

To evaluate the sum, use (20k)=(2020-k). Choosing a total of 20 objects from two disjoint groups of sizes 25 and 20, partition according to how many are chosen from the first group. The partition proves, rather than merely names, the identity

∑k=020(25k)(2020-k)=(4520).

A probabilistic second proof complements the second player's indicators: equal heads means first-player heads plus second-player tails equals 20. Those 45 transformed indicators remain independent and fair, so exactly (4520) detailed outcomes qualify. The index 15 in options two and four counts the wrong target. The denominator 220 in options three and four ignores the first player's 25 independent outcomes; it does not describe their joint experiment. The identity applies to unequal toss counts a,b as (a+bb)/2a+b under independent fair tosses. With unequal coin biases, the weights of the summands change and the fair-count shortcut no longer applies.

Question 5. PhD CS 1404, Q72 — Expected running-minimum updates

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 72. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

An array contains n distinct values in a uniformly random permutation. Set min to positive infinity, scan from index 1 to n, and replace it whenever the next value is smaller. If Y counts replacements, which expression is closest to its mean for large n?

1.

1

2.
lnn
3.

n

4.
nlnn
Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 2. Define Ii to be one when the key at position i is smaller than all earlier keys and zero otherwise. Initialization at positive infinity makes I1=1. Distinct keys and a uniform random permutation imply that each of the first i positions is equally likely to contain the prefix minimum. Hence P(Ii=1)=1/i.

For each permutation, the assignment count satisfies Y=I1+…+In. Adding the expected values gives the exact mean

E[Y]=∑i=1nE[Ii]=∑i=1n1i=Hn.

This step uses linearity, which holds whether or not the indicators are independent; no independence proof is required. Integrating the decreasing function 1/x over successive unit intervals yields ln(n+1)≤Hn≤1+lnn. Thus Hn/lnn→1, explaining the large- n choice lnn. It is an asymptotic approximation, not an exact equality at finite n.

Option one keeps only the compulsory first record. The value n is attained by a decreasing array but is not the mean over all permutations; it is also the number of comparison tests, which remains n for every input. Multiplying that scan length by the expected number of updates produces nlnn, a different quantity with no basis in the requested ledger. If initialization instead uses the first key without counting its assignment, the subsequent record-update mean is Hn-1. Duplicates and nonuniform input distributions require a new symmetry argument.

Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 4. Pre-generate two independent fair bits for each of four coins, even if a second bit is not used. The contribution of coin i is one exactly when its two bits are HH. Thus each contribution has probability 1/4, and contributions from different coins are independent. The other three per-coin outcomes contribute zero.

For exactly two contributions, select their two labels in (42)=6 ways. Every specified successful pair and failed complementary pair has probability (1/4)2(3/4)2. These cases are disjoint, so

P(Y=2)=6116916=27128.

A check by the random eligible count K conditions on the first-round heads:

K P(K) P(Y=2∣K) Joint contribution
2 6/16 1/4 3/32
3 4/16 3/8 3/32

For K<2 the contribution is zero; the three remaining entries sum to 27/128. Treating the second round as four unconditional fair tosses yields 3/8, which belongs to a different experiment. Substituting E[K]=2 for the random count would yield 1/4; expectation does not preserve this probability function. The listed values 1/2, 3/4, and 17/128 fail the exact partition. A particular two-stage outcome has its joint probability before eligibility is conditioned on, which explains the factor 1/4.

Question 7. A probability from exact event cardinalities — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · exact calculation with a required proof extension

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q21; Phd_CS_1404_Q68. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

An equally likely sample space has n+3 outcomes. Event A has n outcomes, B has two, and their intersection has one. Find P(A∪B). Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

Construct all four exact membership regions and verify consistency for every positive integer n. Explain what changes under nonuniform elementary masses.

1.
78
2.
58
3.
18
4.
34
Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 4. At n=5, the uniform space contains eight elementary outcomes. Partition it by membership rather than count the same outcome twice:

Region Count
Both events 1
First only 4
Second only 1
Neither 2

The event union includes the first three rows and has six points, so its mass is 6/8=3/4. Adding the marginals without correction gives option one's 7/8, which counts the shared point twice. Option two's 5/8 counts only A, while option three's 1/8 counts only the intersection. Every point has mass 1/8 by the stated sampling law; the table itself would not justify equal masses without that premise. The construction also shows the given cardinalities are consistent, since all four region counts are nonnegative and total eight. For later generalization, these rows become 1,n-1,1,2, so the union always contains n+1 points, not n+2.

An equally likely sample space has n+3 outcomes. Event A has n outcomes, B has two, and their intersection has one. Find P(A∪B). Calculate the requested quantity for n=8.

Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 3. With n=8, eleven elementary outcomes each have mass 1/11. The four region counts are 1 for both, 8-1=7 for first only, 2-1=1 for second only, and 11-(7+1+1)=2 for neither. Hence

P(A∪B)=7+1+111=911.

The same result follows from subtracting the outside event: 1-2/11=9/11. These two calculations use complementary partitions, providing an independent check on the numerator. Option one counts A alone, option two the overlap alone, and option four uses 8+2=10, which double-counts the common outcome. The exactly-one mass is instead (7+1)/11=8/11; in this special instance it equals the first marginal, but their events are different. Such accidental numeric agreement cannot identify an event. If the two outside points were assigned larger probabilities, their count of two would remain unchanged while the union probability would decrease. Both the atomic partition and the uniform law are required.

Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 2. For every positive integer n, four exact membership counts are 1,n-1,1,2, totaling n+3. The union removes only the final region, so its count is n+1. Under equal elementary masses,

P(A∪B)=n+1n+3=1-2n+3.

This construction proves existence of a model for all stated n≥1, including n=1, where A⊆B and the union mass is 2/4. The complement expression confirms the general count. The numerator n+2 comes from adding both event sizes without subtracting their shared point. The numerator n leaves out the second-only point, and one counts only the overlap. Substitution at n=1 is a boundary check, not the proof of the identity; the partition supplies the universal argument. The result approaches one as n grows because precisely two outside outcomes keep masses 1/(n+3) each. It never equals one for a finite positive n.

Question 10. A probability from exact event cardinalities — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q21; Phd_CS_1404_Q68. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

An equally likely sample space has n+3 outcomes. Event A has n outcomes, B has two, and their intersection has one. Find P(A∪B). Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method?

Construct all four exact membership regions and verify consistency for every positive integer n. Explain what changes under nonuniform elementary masses.

1.

Cardinality ratios require equally likely elementary outcomes.

2.

Counting outcomes gives probabilities under every sample distribution.

3.

An overlap is counted once by adding both events without a correction.

4.

A union must be contained in its intersection.

Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 1. The identity P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B) is valid for any probability law. Replacing probabilities by cardinality ratios is the additional step that requires a finite uniform law. Separate these two statements.

For example, retain the n=5 membership configuration from question seven, but give the two outside points mass 1/4 each and the six union points mass 1/12 each. Total mass is 2(1/4)+6(1/12)=1. The union now has probability 1/2, despite its unchanged cardinality ratio 6/8=3/4. This is a concrete counterexample to option two. Adding both event probabilities without an overlap correction counts the positive shared mass twice, disproving option three. The containment in option four is reversed: A∩B⊆A∪B, and a second-only point witnesses strictness here. Equal likelihood is sufficient for the count rule; exceptional nonuniform laws may produce the same ratio for a particular event, but this does not establish that rule for every event.

Correct option: 4. At n=5, the independent marginals are a=1/5 and b=1/6. Their overlap is ab=1/30. The four atomic masses are

Both First only Second only Neither
1/30 1/6 2/15 2/3

Exactly one selects the middle two cells. Thus P(A△B)=1/6+2/15=5/30+4/30=3/10. All four masses total one, checking the partition. Equivalently, a+b-2ab=1/5+1/6-2/30=9/30.

Option one adds marginals to obtain 11/30, counting both twice. Option two is the overlap 1/30, the event deliberately excluded. Option three is only B∖A with mass 2/15; it omits the first-only alternative. The union mass would be 10/30=1/3, distinct from both the uncorrected sum and exactly one. Under independence the two disjoint exclusive cases have product probabilities a(1-b) and b(1-a); the cases are disjoint even though the original events are not. At general n their sum is (2n-1)/(n(n+1)).

Question 14. Exactly one of two independent events — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q21; Phd_CS_1404_Q68. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Independent events have probabilities 1/n and 1/(n+1). Find the probability that exactly one occurs. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method?

Derive the complete four-cell product law, distinguish union from exactly one, and discuss the endpoint n=1.

1.

Mutual exclusivity and independence are different properties.

2.

Positive-probability mutually exclusive events are independent.

3.

Exactly-one includes the both-event case.

4.

Independence makes the intersection probability zero.

Read the complete atomic model and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 1. Independence is a relation between masses: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). Mutual exclusivity is a relation between sets: A∩B=∅. Here the independent product 1/(n(n+1)) is strictly positive at every finite positive n, proving that these specified events cannot also be mutually exclusive.

More generally, mutually exclusive events are independent only when at least one has zero probability, since 0=P(A)P(B) is then necessary and sufficient. This qualification disproves the positive-probability claim in option two without asserting that disjointness and independence are never compatible. Option three is false because the exactly-one event explicitly removes the intersection. Option four confuses product probability with zero overlap. Quantitatively, independence gives exactly-one probability a+b-2ab, while disjointness would give a+b for consistent disjoint marginals. At n=5, the first is 3/10 and the second 11/30. At n=1, the proposed disjoint marginals even sum to 3/2, exceeding one and making that alternative model impossible.

Question 18. A conditional trial reduced to an indicator — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Correct option: 1. The first-round head count K is random, taking values from zero through n. Conditional on K=k, the second round has exactly k independent fair tosses. Its probability of exactly one head is k/2k for k≥1, and zero for k=0. One may average these conditional probabilities, but cannot replace K by its mean.

For n=2, the eligibility masses are 1/4,1/2,1/4. Hence

P(Y=1)=14·0+12·12+14·24=38.

Option four omits the first-stage requirement: the per-original-coin joint contribution is P(HH)=1/4, although the conditional success probability for an already eligible coin is 1/2. Conditioning and taking a joint event use different denominators. The independent per-coin model automatically averages eligibility and gives the same 2(1/4)(3/4)=3/8.

Correct option: 3. For arbitrary events, separate overlaps before adding masses. Define D1=A1 and Di=Ai∖⋃j<iAj. The sets Di are disjoint and have the same union as the original events. Because Di⊆Ai, monotonicity gives

P(⋃i=1nAi)=∑i=1nP(Di)≤∑i=1nP(Ai).

Here the original sets are already disjoint, so Di=Ai and equality follows. Option one fails for two copies of the same event of probability 1/2: the union mass is 1/2 while the summed bound is one. Option two confuses a union with an intersection and also assumes an unsupported product rule. Option four fails for the positive disjoint masses whenever n≥2. No independence is required for the inequality. Conversely, exact equality in probability need not imply literally empty overlaps: zero-mass intersections do not affect the sum. The given pairwise disjointness is a sufficient, particularly transparent condition for equality.

Question 40. Two events: exactly one and independence

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1405_Q21; Phd_CS_1404_Q68. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

2.
